title: Trend formation with sparse global sampling
authors: Sarath Sankar, Abhijit Sinha, Shankar Ghosh, Vikram Tripathi, Amitava Bhattacharya
abstract: Achieving global coordination without a central controller or dense global communication is a defining challenge for both biological collectives and engineered swarms. We introduce and analyze a minimal model in which self-propelled agents in a bounded domain periodically reorient their motions toward the centroid of a small, randomly chosen subset of their peers, with no direct sensing of any individual neighbor's position or heading. We show that this sparse, non-local sampling rule reliably drives an initially disordered population to a globally aligned, nematic state, and that shrinking the sampled subset -- down to the minimum of two agents -- accelerates ordering rather than impeding it: the resulting estimation noise, filtered through a geometric turning rule, is itself the engine of symmetry breaking. We derive an analytical criterion, in quantitative agreement with simulation, that predicts when this ordering succeeds as a function of the sampling size and sampling frequency. We confirm the mechanism experimentally in a swarm of up to fifteen differential-drive robots. These results identify sparse random sampling as an information-efficient route to collective coordination, with implications for understanding animal collectives and for designing communication-limited robotic swarms.
summary: This work investigates how self-propelled swarms can achieve global order using only sparse, random local information sampling. The authors demonstrate that this sparse sampling is highly efficient, showing that even reducing the sampled subset size can accelerate alignment. The findings establish a theoretical and experimental framework for information-efficient collective coordination.
main_problem: The core challenge is achieving global coordination among self-propelled agents without relying on a central controller or dense global communication.
main_result: Sparse, random sampling is shown to be an information-efficient mechanism that reliably drives disordered populations into a globally aligned, nematic state, with noise playing a constructive role in symmetry breaking.
method: The authors combine analytical derivations of predictive criteria with extensive numerical simulations and physical experiments using differential-drive robots.
model_or_system: The model consists of N point particles (or robots) in 2D, where each agent periodically reorients its motion toward the centroid of a small, randomly sampled subset of its peers.
key_observables: Nematic Order Parameter (S(t)), Circular Variance, and Trend Formation Time (t_f).
important_parameters: Sampling size (n), sampling frequency, and the reorientation threshold ($R_T = \sqrt{N}$).
main_assumptions: The dynamics are modeled as collisionless point-particle motion, and the experimental setup maps this idealized model onto physical robots using non-overlapping offsets.
figures_summary: Figures compare the evolution of alignment (nematic order) and the time required to reach alignment ($t_f$) when using different sampling sizes ($n=2$ vs. $n=[\sqrt{N}]$), demonstrating that smaller samples accelerate ordering.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the minimal model dynamics, to analyzing the role of sampling size on ordering metrics, deriving analytical criteria, and finally validating these findings through physical robot experiments.
why_interesting: The concept of using inherent estimation noise (fluctuations) as the driving force for spontaneous symmetry breaking and collective order is a general principle applicable to non-equilibrium statistical physics and complex systems.
